stories.headline: Update: Federal Judge Blocks Most DHS Field Operations Focused on Voter Fraud in Nine States
stories.summary:
A federal judge in California on Wednesday blocked most Department of Homeland Security field operations focused on voter fraud. U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, appointed under former President Joe Biden, barred DHS from conducting "elections-related field operations and field interviews" in nine states, including California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York and Pennsylvania.

The ruling largely halts a sprawling effort in which agents knocked on doors to ask residents about their immigration status and whether they had voted in recent elections, as part of a search for noncitizens registered to vote. The judge found the practice likely violates the Voting Rights Act.

The decision arrives roughly two weeks before the midterm elections and follows recent reports of armed federal agents visiting homes in search of noncitizen voters. Supporters of the operations have framed them as a necessary effort to protect election integrity and enforce existing law against illegal voting. Critics, including voting rights advocates, have argued that the door-knocking intimidates eligible voters and exceeds DHS authority.

The ruling is a court order issued in a legal challenge to the program, and an appeal by the administration is a possible next step. The case will be closely watched for its effect on how federal agencies operate around the November vote.

stories.headline: Two Killed in Houthi Attack on Airport in Eastern Saudi Arabia
stories.summary:
Yemen's Houthi movement said it attacked an airport in eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, and Saudi authorities said the strike killed two people and injured eight at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam. The Saudi civil aviation authority identified the dead as a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident. The Houthis said the airport was among several sites targeted with drones and missiles over the previous 48 hours.

Separately, two more people were killed Wednesday morning by debris from a drone intercepted over Eastern Province, according to the Saudi energy ministry. The drone had been aimed at an Aramco processing facility in the Shaybah oil field. The Saudi-led coalition said four more drones were intercepted over Riyadh and Medina on Thursday.

At least 21 people have been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities. A missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 and injured 308, the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade. The US has ordered some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia, and the UK is deploying jets to help defend the kingdom.

The Houthis say the attacks are retaliation for Saudi air strikes in territory they control. The Houthi-run health ministry says 155 civilians have been killed since fighting flared three months ago, while the Yemeni government puts total deaths at at least 1,574. More than 256,000 people have been displaced. Egypt has said it is prepared to give Saudi Arabia military assistance, while its foreign minister urged political solutions.

stories.headline: First Human Case of Shamonda Virus Detected in France
stories.summary:
French authorities announced the first known human case of the Shamonda virus, found in a patient who died in early October. Health officials described it as an "exceptional case in a severely immunocompromised patient" and said there is currently no risk to the public. The virus mainly affects cattle and is spread by infected midges.

The patient was treated at a Lyon hospital for a serious illness and developed neurological complications "very likely linked" to the virus, according to initial findings. Officials believe the person was bitten by a midge in eastern France, where animal cases were first identified in the spring. Until now the virus was considered non-transmissible to humans despite decades of circulation in Africa and Asia.

The World Health Organization confirmed this is the first documented human case. It has not yet made a formal risk assessment but said the case appears isolated and is unlikely to lead to wider spread, noting that midge-borne virus transmission generally declines in cooler months. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control is working with French and European partners on the potential public health implications.

The virus was first identified in Europe in late July and has since been found in farm animals in Ireland, Germany, Italy, Spain and Jersey. French officials are still investigating how the infection reached a human.

stories.headline: Screwworm Detected in Texas Wildlife for First Time, USDA Says
stories.summary:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture said the New World screwworm has been detected in an elk found on a game ranch in Pecos County, Texas, marking its spread to U.S. wildlife. The parasitic fly can enter animals through open wounds and feed on living tissue.

The finding is significant because the pest has been a major concern for the American livestock industry, and detection in wildlife complicates containment efforts. Wild animals move freely and are harder to monitor and treat than cattle on managed ranches.

Federal and state agricultural officials are expected to continue surveillance and response measures in the area. Further details on any quarantine or treatment steps were not immediately available in the reporting.

stories.headline: AI-Discovered PHP Flaws Trigger Global Cyber-Security Scramble
stories.summary:
Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are working to contain the fallout from serious vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, a programming language used since the 2000s to build websites. The flaws had gone undetected for more than a decade and were uncovered with the help of artificial intelligence. Security firm Wiz, whose researchers helped find them, called them the "most severe" ever detected by AI, while OpenAI, whose technology was used in the discovery, described them as "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory."

PHP powers a vast range of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress. According to the reporting, the main flaw could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and to steal sensitive data. Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, estimated that it could affect "millions and millions" of websites. Researcher Jill Slay of the University of Adelaide said it would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw.

The alert has disrupted services worldwide, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums. Wikimedia took down a number of its systems as a precaution. The Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC took sites or pages offline, the Dutch cyber-security agency pulled its website, and several Scottish councils and health boards did the same.

PHP developers released patches on Wednesday and urged all users to update immediately. Authorities have advised website operators to install the emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline. Researcher Salil Kanhere of UNSW Sydney warned that more exploitation attempts are likely in the coming weeks now that the technical details are public, with smaller organisations and poorly maintained sites at greatest risk.

stories.headline: Update: Russia Frees American Stephen Hubbard as Witkoff Meets Putin; Praise for Putin Draws Republican Criticism
stories.summary:
Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American and former teacher from Michigan, as President Vladimir Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg early Wednesday. Hubbard was sentenced in 2024 to almost seven years in a penal colony for allegedly fighting for Ukraine, after being captured in 2022. The State Department had classified him as wrongfully detained. CBS News reported he was in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.

President Donald Trump said Hubbard was "on his way back home" and that "there was no 'swap' necessary," saying he had asked Putin directly for the release last week. Most past releases of Americans from Russia came through prisoner swaps. Trump also appeared to link the outcome to his recent decision to suspend sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, writing that had sanctions been imposed, negotiations "would have come to a complete and total halt."

Witkoff told Putin, "you are a humanitarian also sir, and I salute that," prompting criticism from within the president's own party. Representative Don Bacon called it "another embarrassment," and Senator John Cornyn said Putin "is a stone cold killer." Vice President JD Vance defended the envoy, saying he cared "much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."

The release comes as the administration pursues talks on ending the war in Ukraine, with Putin having agreed in principle to resume trilateral negotiations after an earlier Witkoff meeting. Critics question whether concessions such as the sanctions suspension are warranted, while supporters point to the return of an American held for years.

stories.headline: Update: Omar Says She Must Move After Threats Following Federal Search of Her Home
stories.summary:
Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, said she will have to move out of her Washington, D.C., apartment because of threats she has received since federal agents executed a search warrant at her residence last week. The search was part of an immigration fraud investigation. "Obviously, I can't continue to live there," Omar said, noting that her address has become public.

Omar said her husband and son were home when federal agents began banging on the doors at 6 a.m., and that agents then conducted a search lasting several hours. Reuters and Fox News reported on the raid when it occurred on October 12.

The case has become politically charged ahead of the midterm elections. Omar's critics have pointed to the immigration fraud probe as grounds for scrutiny of a sitting member of Congress, while her allies and many Democrats have framed the search as politically motivated and have raised concerns about the safety of lawmakers. The article provides few further details on the investigation itself, and no charges against Omar were mentioned.

The development is the first concrete follow-up on the search, showing its personal and security consequences for a member of Congress and her family. The investigation remains ongoing.

stories.headline: Irish Government Issues State Apology to Family of Prison Officer Killed by IRA
stories.summary:
Taoiseach Micheal Martin delivered a formal state apology to the family of Brian Stack, a senior Irish prison officer murdered by the IRA, during a sitting of the Dail on Wednesday. The apology was for failings in the investigations into his killing. Stack, a father of three and chief prison officer at the high-security Portlaoise Prison, was shot in the back of the neck in Dublin in 1983 after leaving a boxing match. He was left paralysed and died 18 months later at age 49.

Three separate garda investigations were carried out, but no one has been brought to justice. Martin said the Provisional IRA is "still in the possession of all the facts" in the case. Stack's wife Sheila and sons Austin, Kieran and Oliver attended the chamber.

The brothers walked out when Sinn Fein TDs spoke. Austin Stack said Sinn Fein leader Mary Lou McDonald, who was absent, has consistently said the IRA campaign was justified, and he called on her to address the family's concerns. McDonald, who was being interviewed by the Police Service of Northern Ireland over protests at Garvaghy Road, welcomed the apology and said the IRA had acknowledged responsibility and expressed sorrow more than a decade ago.

A Sinn Fein spokesperson said the party was deeply sorry for the family's loss, acknowledged the hurt caused by past republican actions, and said investigating the killing is a matter for An Garda Siochana.
